source.title: Evaluating Language Models for Efficient Code Generation
source.authors: Jiawei Liu; Songrun Xie; Junhao Wang; Yuxiang Wei; Yifeng Ding; Lingming Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study compares code-generation efficiency across model sizes and reports that the trend is inconsistent, explicitly saying the scaling law does not seem explicit for code efficiency. This refines the downstream-predictability version, but it does not test pretraining cross-entropy scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper measures the efficiency of generated code, not held-out language-model loss or compute-optimal allocation. Rows cover only model-size comparisons relevant to downstream predictability (V6); cited language-model scaling results and the study's other efficiency findings are not rows for the other versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream code-generation results (efficiency DPS and pass@1) across sizes within released model families. It states that the scaling law 'does not seem explicit for code efficiency'. That is a specific argument that V6 needs restating for this downstream measure. It fits no loss curves and does not measure pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say the Kaplan scaling law persists for code correctness but 'does not seem explicit' for code efficiency: 7 of 12 larger models improve and 4 degrade. They also note, in the appendix, reversed scaling of CodeLlama pass@1 on EvalPerf tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares generated-code efficiency across model sizes using DPS; it does not measure the original studies' held-out loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size trend varies across model families and model variants (instruct versus base).
record.problems: The model-size findings report pairwise outcomes and counts without uncertainty estimates for those comparisons. The paper's metric is generated-code efficiency, not pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 contains further pairwise values, but they are not individually transcribed because the flattened figure layout does not support reliable assignment of every value to a model pair. The overall reported count and the explicitly described comparisons are retained in R1–R4.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss is measured.
All: no fits and no extrapolation.
All: no other modalities or training regimes are fitted.
Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted functional trend; controlled scaling with training held fixed.

missing.what: Correctness pass@1 by model size (HE+, MBPP+, EvalPerf) for each family, e.g. CodeLlama base HE+ 35.9/38.7/44.0/50.2 at 7B/13B/34B/70B. Includes the reversed CodeLlama EvalPerf pass@1 trend (instruct 86.9/88.9/88.1/81.7).
DPS by size computed over each model's own passing tasks (not the common set), e.g. StarCoder2 base 80.5/73.8/82.1 at 3B/7B/15B.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak test of V6. It uses pairwise comparisons of off-the-shelf models whose training data and tokens differ across sizes, fits no curve, and reports no uncertainty. The paper's main contribution is the DPE benchmark, and its methodology results (Tables 1-2) are rightly not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests model-size predictability for code-generation efficiency, but not downstream performance generally or predictability from pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-instruct vs DeepSeekCoder-1.3B-instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-efficiency DPS across model sizes within a family.

conditions.value: instruct variants; common set of passing solutions

rows.measure: Differential Performance Score (DPS) for code efficiency
rows.value: DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-instruct improves the DPS of the 1.3B version by 14%.
rows.note: Pairwise comparison as described by the authors.
rows.check: Value is correct (14% DPS gain, 1.3B to 6.7B instruct, Fig. 5). Confound: family members differ in more than parameter count, so this is not a controlled scaling run.

rows.subject: StarCoder2 15B vs StarCoder2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-efficiency DPS across model sizes within a family.

conditions.value: base variants; common set of passing solutions

rows.measure: Differential Performance Score (DPS) for code efficiency
rows.value: There is an 8.7% improvement from StarCoder2 7B to 15B.
rows.note: Pairwise comparison as described by the authors.
rows.check: Value is correct (8.7% gain, StarCoder2 7B to 15B base). Same confound as R1.

rows.subject: StarCoder2 7B vs StarCoder2 3B
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-efficiency DPS across model sizes within a family.

conditions.value: base variants; common set of passing solutions

rows.measure: Differential Performance Score (DPS) for code efficiency
rows.value: In the worst case, there is a 6% degradation between the 3B and 7B versions of StarCoder2 base models.
rows.note: The text identifies the 3B-to-7B comparison as the worst degradation.
rows.check: Value is correct (6% degradation, StarCoder2 3B to 7B base). Table 3 agrees: DPS avg 80.5 vs 73.8, on each model's own passing tasks.

rows.subject: 12 within-family model-size pairs (CodeLlama-instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-instruct, and StarCoder2-base)
rows.stage_stated: varies by family: instruct or base
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairwise code-efficiency DPS across sizes within model families.
rows.value: Within the 12 pairs in Figure 5, there are seven cases where a larger model in the family outperforms the smaller one; performance degradation with > 1% loss also happens 4 times.
rows.note: The authors report these counts across the 12 pairs; individual outcomes beyond the named examples are not enumerated in the prose.
rows.check: Counts are correct: 7 of 12 pairs improve and 4 degrade by more than 1%. The 12 pairs are 6 CodeLlama, 3 DeepSeek and 3 StarCoder2. No uncertainty is reported.

relationships.reason: The larger model has higher DPS on the common passing set (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: DPS increased from DeepSeek-Coder-instruct 1.3B to 6.7B and StarCoder2-base 7B to 15B on their common passing sets.

relationships.reason: The larger model's DPS is 6% lower (R3).
relationships.display_finding: The larger model's DPS was 6% lower.

relationships.condition: Code-efficiency DPS across all 12 within-family size pairs
relationships.reason: Only 7 of 12 larger models improve and 4 degrade by more than 1%, so efficiency does not track size consistently (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Only 7 of 12 larger models improved code efficiency, while 4 degraded by more than 1%.

relationships.condition: pass@1 on the 121 EvalPerf tasks, CodeLlama family (from text; no row)
relationships.reason: Appendix A.3 and Table 3 report reversed scaling: CodeLlama-70B-instruct scores 81.7 vs 86.9 for 7B. No row records this.
relationships.display_finding: CodeLlama-70B-instruct scored 81.7 on pass@1, below 86.9 for 7B across 121 EvalPerf tasks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Code-efficiency DPS improves with the larger model in these reported comparisons (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The larger model has a reported 6% DPS degradation in this comparison (R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Larger models outperform smaller ones in seven cases, but four cases show degradation greater than 1%, so efficiency does not improve consistently with size in these tested comparisons (R4).
